questions.stem: 52-year-old with well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes (A1C 6.8%) is scheduled for knee arthroscopy at a freestanding surgery center. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Appropriate if his conditions stay medically stable
Appropriate if he is reclassified as ASA 1
Inappropriate because diabetes excludes ambulatory care
Inappropriate because ASA 3 patients need a hospital
questions.explanation: Ambulatory surgery mostly serves ASA 1 and 2 patients, and ASA 3 or 4 patients are acceptable when their systemic disease is medically stable. Stable diabetes and hypertension don't exclude him. Reclassifying an ASA status doesn't change risk, and no rule bars ASA 3 patients from surgery centers.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which case is BEST suited to a freestanding ambulatory surgery center?
options: Open colectomy needing overnight pain control
Elective carpal tunnel release in an ASA 2 adult
Emergency appendectomy in a septic patient
Scheduled cesarean delivery in a healthy parturient
questions.explanation: Ambulatory cases are elective, carry low rates of postoperative complications, and don't need an overnight stay. Obstetric cases are excluded from ambulatory settings. An open colectomy needs inpatient care, and an emergency in a septic patient needs hospital resources.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are recognized advantages of ambulatory surgery centers? (Select 3)
options: Wider presence in rural and inner-city areas
Lower costs because they don't subsidize costlier hospital services
questions.explanation: ASCs avoid subsidizing expensive hospital services, schedule more predictably, and turn rooms over faster, which also saves Medicare money. They tend to serve insured patients, for-profit centers rarely provide charity or subsidized care, and they are seldom located in rural or inner-city areas.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: A hospital lost emergency coverage for one surgical specialty after that group moved to a freestanding center. Which disadvantages of ASCs does this illustrate or accompany? (Select 2)
options: Higher overall cost per case than hospitals
Loss of specialty coverage for the hospital's emergency department
Preference for insured over uninsured patients
questions.explanation: A specialty working only in a freestanding center can leave the hospital ED without coverage, and ASCs tend to serve insured patients rather than uninsured ones. Lower cost, predictable scheduling, fast turnover, and Medicare savings are advantages, not disadvantages.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 48-year-old with diagnosed severe OSA on home CPAP is scheduled for carpal tunnel release under a regional block at an ASC. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Unacceptable because severe OSA excludes ambulatory surgery
Unacceptable unless the AHI has improved on recent sleep study
Acceptable for this kind of case and technique
Acceptable if converted to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: For patients with OSA, a procedure typically done as an outpatient under local or regional anesthesia is acceptable for an ASC. Severe OSA alone doesn't exclude him. General anesthesia raises airway and opioid risk rather than lowering it. A repeat sleep study isn't required for this decision.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Infant born at 34 weeks' gestation is now 18 weeks old and scheduled for hernia repair. What is the postconceptual age, and what does it imply?
options: 46 weeks; monitor 12 hr after surgery for apnea
18 weeks; no extra monitoring is needed
52 weeks; monitor 12 hr after surgery for apnea
questions.explanation: Postconceptual age = gestational age at birth + postnatal age: 34 + 18 = 52 weeks. For preterm infants, PCA under 60 weeks warrants 12 hr of postoperative monitoring for apnea. 46 weeks uses the term-infant cutoff as if it were the age. Postnatal age alone ignores prematurity.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Term infant (born at 40 weeks) is now 4 weeks old and scheduled for circumcision. Which statement is BEST?
options: PCA 44 weeks; monitor for 12 hr postop
PCA 56 weeks; monitor because he is under 60 weeks
PCA 44 weeks; discharge after standard PACU criteria
questions.explanation: 40 + 4 = 44 weeks. Term infants under 46 weeks PCA need about 12 hr of monitoring for apnea. Standard discharge ignores apnea risk. Postnatal age alone isn't the measure. The 60-week cutoff applies to preterm infants, and 56 is a miscalculation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Infant born at 39 weeks is now 10 weeks old for an outpatient procedure. What is the BEST plan regarding apnea monitoring?
questions.explanation: 39 + 10 = 49 weeks, which is past the 46-week threshold for term infants, so extended apnea monitoring isn't routinely needed. The 60-week threshold applies to preterm infants. Postnatal age alone ignores gestation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Infant born at 30 weeks is now 26 weeks old and scheduled for eye examination under anesthesia as an outpatient. What does PCA imply?
options: PCA 66 weeks; monitor 12 hr for apnea
PCA 26 weeks; routine discharge is reasonable
PCA 56 weeks; monitor 12 hr for apnea
PCA 56 weeks; routine discharge is reasonable
questions.explanation: 30 + 26 = 56 weeks, under the 60-week threshold for preterm infants, so 12 hr of monitoring is indicated. 66 is an arithmetic error. Postnatal age alone misses the prematurity risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 4-year-old with a runny nose is scheduled for ear tubes. Which factors are independent risks for adverse respiratory events with a URI? (Select 4)
options: Endotracheal tube rather than a face mask or LMA
questions.explanation: ETT use, prematurity, reactive airway disease, parental smoking, airway surgery, and copious secretions or congestion independently raise risk. Clear rhinorrhea in an active child isn't on the list. Extremity surgery isn't airway surgery.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 3-year-old for tympanostomy has clear rhinorrhea, eats and plays normally, temp 37.0 °C, RR 24, and looks well. What is the BEST plan?
options: Proceed with a planned endotracheal tube
Cancel and obtain a chest X-ray first
Proceed with a mask or LMA technique
questions.explanation: A child with a URI who is afebrile, active, eating normally, with a normal RR, and not ill-appearing can generally proceed, and avoiding an ETT lowers risk. A 6-week delay applies to adults after viral URIs. An ETT is itself a risk factor. A chest film isn't needed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 3-year-old for tympanostomy has a URI with temp 38.6 °C, thick green nasal discharge, wet cough, and decreased appetite. What is the BEST plan?
options: Proceed with glycopyrrolate to dry secretions
Proceed with an LMA to avoid intubation
questions.explanation: Fever, purulent secretions, cough, and reduced activity or appetite suggest active illness, and postponing is reasonable. An LMA or glycopyrrolate reduces some risk but doesn't make an ill child an appropriate elective candidate. Deep extubation adds laryngospasm risk in a child with secretions.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 35-year-old had a viral URI that resolved 2 weeks ago and is scheduled for elective septoplasty. Which plan BEST reflects airway physiology?
options: Proceed with deep extubation to avoid coughing at emergence
Proceed; symptoms resolved, so reactivity has too
questions.explanation: In adults, airway hyperreactivity and airflow obstruction persist for up to 6 weeks after a viral URI, so delaying elective airway surgery to that point is reasonable. Symptom resolution doesn't mean reactivity has resolved. Three weeks is too short. Deep extubation doesn't remove the hyperreactivity.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Adult had a viral URI ending on March 1 and wants elective sinus surgery as soon as reasonable. Using a 6-week window, what is the earliest date?
questions.explanation: 6 weeks after March 1 is about April 12. March 15 is 2 weeks, March 29 is 4 weeks, and May 10 is about 10 weeks.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements about anesthetic technique for ambulatory surgery are accurate? (Select 3)
options: Sore throat is more common after spinal than general
Regional anesthesia shortens PACU stay compared with general alone
General, regional, and local anesthesia are comparably safe
Regional plus general shortens PACU stay compared with general alone
Spinal anesthesia speeds discharge in ambulatory patients
Regional anesthesia has no failure rate to plan for
questions.explanation: All three techniques are considered equally safe, and adding regional shortens PACU stay. Regional blocks have a failure rate that needs a backup plan. Spinal can lengthen discharge if voiding is required. Sore throat and nausea are more common after general anesthesia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 30-year-old receives a spinal for outpatient knee arthroscopy. In PACU she meets other discharge criteria but hasn't voided. Which statement BEST reflects current evidence?
options: Voiding is a mandatory criterion after any spinal
She needs a urinary catheter before discharge
Discharge is acceptable once motor block wears off, with no further assessment
Voiding may be required for selected higher-risk patients
questions.explanation: Voiding can delay discharge after spinal anesthesia, but ASA guidance says it shouldn't be a routine discharge requirement; it is reasonable for selected patients, such as those with long-acting spinals, urologic or hernia surgery, or prior retention, who often get a bladder scan. Discrepancy flag: a note in the course materials states a spinal patient has to urinate before discharge, which is stricter than current guidance. Discharge still requires assessment, and a catheter isn't needed in an asymptomatic patient.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Compared with general anesthesia for outpatient surgery, which outcomes favor spinal anesthesia? (Select 2)
options: Faster discharge when voiding is required
questions.explanation: Sore throat and nausea are more common after general anesthesia. Spinal carries PDPH risk (similar overall headache rates with small needles), may cause backache, and can delay voiding and discharge.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient population should NOT be scheduled at a freestanding ambulatory surgery center?
options: Healthy children over 6 months for ear tubes
Adults with stable hypertension for cataract surgery
questions.explanation: Obstetric cases and parturients are excluded from ambulatory settings because of the need for maternal and fetal resources. The other patients are typical ambulatory candidates.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are the two primary anesthetic concerns that drive ambulatory technique choices? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Fast emergence and low PONV rates are the two main ambulatory priorities. Cost, monitoring, surgeon preference, and fasting matter but aren't the two core concerns.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Two ambulatory patients wake within 5 min of the end of surgery. One leaves PACU in 40 min; the other stays 3 hr. Which factor BEST explains the difference?
options: Use of a regional block in the first patient
Nausea and vomiting in the second patient
questions.explanation: Fast wake-up doesn't guarantee a short PACU stay. Nausea, with or without vomiting, is the factor most likely to delay discharge and cause unplanned admission. Anesthetic choice, blocks, and surgery length matter less once both patients are awake.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: What factor is MOST likely to delay discharge or cause unplanned admission after ambulatory surgery?
options: A small amount of surgical-site discomfort
questions.explanation: Nausea and vomiting are the leading causes of delayed discharge and unanticipated admission after ambulatory surgery. Mild shivering, a slow emergence, and mild pain are usually manageable.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Outpatient leaves the surgery center at 4 pm and develops bleeding at 10 pm, after the center closes. What should have been addressed before discharge?
options: An overnight stay for every ASC patient
Where to go for after-hours problems
questions.explanation: Most ASCs aren't open around the clock, so patients need clear instructions on where to return or seek care if a complication occurs. An overnight stay isn't required for each patient, and opioids or routine labs don't address the problem.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes wake-up time from discharge time after ambulatory anesthesia?
options: A faster wake-up doesn't by itself shorten PACU stay
Wake-up time determines discharge in most patients
Discharge depends mainly on the anesthetic agent used
Discharge time is fixed at twice the wake-up time
questions.explanation: Wake-up and discharge are distinct; pain and PONV control drive faster recovery and discharge more than emergence speed. The other statements overstate the link.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which measures BEST support faster recovery and discharge after ambulatory surgery? (Select 3)
options: Long-acting opioids as the main analgesic
questions.explanation: Pain control, PONV prevention, and regional techniques shorten recovery. Deeper anesthesia, routine overnight stays, and long-acting opioids work against fast discharge.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which BEST defines ambulatory anesthesia?
options: Anesthesia delivered with local or regional techniques
Anesthesia delivered outside a hospital building
Anesthesia delivered by a single provider without assistance
questions.explanation: Ambulatory anesthesia means same-day arrival and discharge from the surgical venue, which may be hospital-based, freestanding, or office-based. Location outside a hospital defines OBA or freestanding centers, not ambulatory care itself.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement about ASC locations is MOST accurate?
options: They're limited to sites inside a licensed hospital
They can't be affiliated with a parent hospital
They may be hospital-based or freestanding
questions.explanation: ASCs can be hospital-based or freestanding satellite facilities affiliated with or independent of a hospital, often on or near the hospital campus. NORA refers to sites inside a hospital outside the OR. Office-based practices are a separate category.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Obese patient (BMI 44) with untreated suspected OSA is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA at a freestanding center. What is the BEST plan?
options: Cancel permanently; obese patients can't have ambulatory surgery
Proceed; obesity isn't a factor in ambulatory outcomes
Assess OSA risk; consider a monitored setting
questions.explanation: Obese patients are more likely to have adverse outcomes and OSA, so risk assessment, optimization, and possibly a setting with postoperative monitoring are needed. Obesity does affect outcomes. Opioid-heavy plans raise risk. Obesity alone doesn't permanently exclude ambulatory surgery.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which children with URI symptoms have additional risk for perioperative respiratory events? (Select 3)
options: Child with clear rhinorrhea, afebrile, and active
Child having inguinal hernia repair under a caudal block and mask
questions.explanation: Reactive airway disease, prematurity, and airway surgery are independent risk factors. A well-appearing child, nonsmoking household, and a mask-based technique for non-airway surgery lower risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which technique change MOST lowers respiratory risk for a child with a URI having a short, non-airway procedure?
options: Using an LMA or face mask instead of an ETT
Giving a larger opioid dose to blunt airway reflexes
Using an ETT to protect the airway from secretions
Deep extubation of an ETT to avoid coughing
questions.explanation: Endotracheal intubation is an independent risk factor, so an LMA or mask lowers risk. Deep extubation and larger opioid doses don't reduce the URI-related risk and may increase it.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement about ASC patient selection by age is MOST accurate?
options: No pediatric patients can have ambulatory surgery
questions.explanation: Age matters most for infants, where postconceptual age determines apnea risk and monitoring. Children and older adults routinely have ambulatory surgery when otherwise appropriate.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why do former preterm infants have a higher postconceptual age threshold for apnea monitoring than term infants?
options: They metabolize volatile agents faster than term infants
Their respiratory control is less mature
questions.explanation: Immature brainstem control of breathing makes former preterm infants prone to postoperative apnea up to a higher PCA (under 60 weeks). The other statements don't explain apnea risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which findings support proceeding with elective surgery in a child with a mild URI? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: A well-appearing, afebrile child with normal activity, appetite, and RR can generally proceed. Wheezing and purulent secretions suggest lower airway involvement or bacterial infection.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: ASA 4 patient with unstable angina is scheduled for cystoscopy at a freestanding surgery center. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Appropriate if the patient has an escort
Appropriate under MAC with no extra preparation
Appropriate because the procedure is minor
Not until his cardiac status is stabilized
questions.explanation: ASA 3 or 4 patients are acceptable only when their systemic disease is medically stable. Unstable angina isn't stable. A minor procedure or MAC doesn't remove the cardiac risk. An escort is required but doesn't address stability.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the speaker-note findings comparing spinal and general anesthesia for outpatients?
options: Spinal had lower cost and length of stay in those studies
Headache was much more common after spinal with small needles
Spinal had higher cost because of longer PACU stays
Nausea was more common after spinal
questions.explanation: Spinal anesthesia was associated with lower costs and length of stay. With small needles, headache incidence is similar after either technique. Nausea and sore throat are more common after general anesthesia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with a history of severe PONV is having outpatient breast surgery. Which approach BEST serves the main ambulatory goals?
options: Regional block, propofol TIVA, and multimodal prophylaxis
Deep volatile anesthetic to ensure no recall
Volatile anesthetic with long-acting opioids for postoperative comfort
questions.explanation: Regional techniques, propofol-based anesthesia, and multimodal prophylaxis reduce PONV and speed discharge. Volatiles and opioids raise PONV risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient has an ASC procedure that typically requires an overnight stay for pain control. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: It is acceptable for ASA 1 patients
It is acceptable if a family member stays overnight with the patient
It isn't appropriate for a freestanding ambulatory center
It is acceptable if a long-acting block is placed
questions.explanation: Ambulatory procedures shouldn't require an overnight stay; those that do belong in a setting that provides one. A family member, block, or ASA class doesn't change the inpatient need.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which payment advantage is attributed to ambulatory surgery centers?
options: They are reimbursed by private insurers alone
They receive higher Medicare rates than hospitals
Medicare saves money on procedures done there
questions.explanation: ASCs lower costs, and Medicare saves money on procedures performed there. They do bill Medicare, typically at lower rates than hospital outpatient departments.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with a URI 3 weeks ago has persistent mild cough and is scheduled for elective bronchoscopy. Which concern is MOST relevant?
options: Higher risk of postoperative urinary retention
questions.explanation: Airway hyperreactivity persists for weeks after a viral URI and increases bronchospasm and laryngospasm risk, especially with airway instrumentation. The other concerns aren't linked to URIs.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which characteristics define an appropriate ambulatory surgical procedure? (Select 3)
options: No need for an overnight stay
questions.explanation: Ambulatory procedures are elective, have low complication rates, pose little safety risk, and don't require an overnight stay. ICU admission, major blood loss, and inpatient analgesia point to inpatient surgery.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Ambulatory patient received a regional block plus light general anesthesia. Compared with general anesthesia alone, what PACU outcome should you expect?
options: Longer PACU stay because of the block
Longer stay because of block-related nausea
questions.explanation: Regional plus general anesthesia shortens PACU stay compared with general alone, largely through better analgesia and less opioid use. Blocks don't typically cause nausea.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which pediatric URI finding MOST strongly suggests postponing elective surgery?
options: Mild nasal congestion without fever or cough
questions.explanation: Fever and purulent secretions suggest more significant illness. Clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, and mild congestion in an otherwise well child generally allow proceeding.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with poorly controlled asthma had a viral URI 10 days ago and is scheduled for elective hernia repair. What is the BEST approach?
options: Proceed with an ETT to secure the airway
Proceed with desflurane for faster recovery
Proceed after a single albuterol treatment
questions.explanation: Recent URI plus poorly controlled reactive airway disease raises bronchospasm risk; delaying and optimizing is reasonable for elective surgery. An ETT and desflurane increase airway irritation. A single albuterol dose doesn't reverse ongoing hyperreactivity.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which infant is LEAST likely to need extended postoperative apnea monitoring?
questions.explanation: Term infants over 46 weeks PCA don't need routine extended monitoring. Term infants under 46 weeks and preterm infants under 60 weeks do.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why might a for-profit freestanding ASC be absent from a rural community?
options: Rural patients can't have ambulatory surgery
They locate where insured patients are
Rural hospitals offer ASC services instead
questions.explanation: For-profit facilities tend to locate where insured patients are and seldom serve rural or inner-city areas. No regulation bans rural ASCs, and rural patients can have ambulatory surgery.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which questions should be asked before scheduling a patient at an ASC? (Select 4)
options: Has the patient had surgery at a hospital before?
For infants, what is the postconceptual age?
Is the patient's systemic disease medically stable?
Does the patient have OSA, and what technique is planned?
Does the patient prefer morning or afternoon surgery?
Is the case elective with low complication risk?
questions.explanation: Case type, patient stability, OSA with planned technique, and infant PCA determine ambulatory suitability. Time preference and prior hospital surgery don't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 7-year-old with a mild URI, parents who smoke, and asthma is scheduled for adenotonsillectomy. Which plan is MOST reasonable?
options: Proceed with an LMA for tonsillectomy
Proceed; a URI alone isn't a risk factor
Consider postponing given multiple risk factors
Proceed with deep extubation to avoid coughing at emergence
questions.explanation: Parental smoking, reactive airway disease, and airway surgery are independent risk factors that add to URI risk, making postponement reasonable. Deep extubation doesn't remove the risk. An LMA is possible for tonsillectomy but doesn't eliminate the combined risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST explains why spinal anesthesia may lengthen discharge?
options: Higher PONV than general anesthesia in outpatients
The need to confirm voiding in selected patients
questions.explanation: Spinal can delay discharge when voiding is required. Consciousness isn't affected, PONV is lower than with general anesthesia, and oral intake isn't delayed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which measure BEST reduces unplanned admissions after ambulatory surgery?
questions.explanation: PONV is the leading cause of unanticipated admission; preventing and treating it reduces admissions. Longer observation doesn't address the cause. Deeper anesthesia and routine IV opioids worsen PONV.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients are typical ASC candidates by ASA class? (Select 2)
options: ASA 4 patient with decompensated heart failure
ASA 3 patient with poorly controlled diabetes and DKA history this week
ASA 2 patient with mild asthma for arthroscopy
questions.explanation: ASA 1 and 2 patients are typical; ASA 3 and 4 patients qualify only when medically stable. Decompensated, unstable, or poorly controlled disease excludes them.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which ambulatory facility type can be located on or near a hospital campus while operating separately?
questions.explanation: Surgery centers may be outside the hospital but affiliated with it and located near or on the same campus. Office rooms aren't hospital-affiliated, and NORA sites are inside the hospital.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which considerations apply to ambulatory surgery in children with recent URI? (Select 2)
options: An ETT protects better against laryngospasm
Children with URIs need 6-week delays in every case
Postponement is reasonable with fever or purulent secretions
Avoiding an ETT when possible lowers risk
questions.explanation: Avoiding intubation lowers risk, and ill-appearing children with fever or purulent secretions should be postponed. The distractors are incorrect or overstated.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: A plastic surgeon performs liposuction in a freestanding procedure room that isn't accredited as an ASC or hospital. How is this setting classified?
options: Non-operating room anesthesia within a hospital
questions.explanation: OBA takes place in a freestanding medical or surgical office or procedure room not accredited as an ASC or hospital. NORA refers to sites outside the OR but inside a licensed hospital. The other options require hospital or ASC accreditation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Anesthesia is provided for an MRI in the radiology department of a licensed hospital. How is this setting classified?
questions.explanation: NORA is any anesthetic outside a traditional OR but within a fully licensed hospital, including MRI, endoscopy, interventional radiology, and ECT. OBA is outside accredited facilities. Class A refers to an office classification.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which locations are typical NORA sites? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: NORA sites lie within a licensed hospital but outside the OR: endoscopy, IR, MRI, and ECT. Freestanding dental or cosmetic offices are office-based settings.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Closed claims data compare injuries in offices and ASCs. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Office injuries were more often permanent or fatal
Injury severity was similar in both settings
Office injuries were mostly temporary and nondisabling
ASC injuries were more often permanent or fatal
questions.explanation: About 64% of office injuries were permanent or led to death versus about 21% in ASCs, where 62% were temporary and nondisabling. Office injuries were only 21% temporary.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In the office-based closed claims data, about what percentage of reported injuries were temporary and nondisabling?
questions.explanation: About 21% of office injuries were temporary and nondisabling and about 64% were permanent or fatal. 62% describes temporary injuries in ASCs. 34% is the fatality share among MAC injuries.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In the ASC closed claims data, about what percentage of injuries were permanent or led to death?
questions.explanation: In ASCs about 62% of injuries were temporary and nondisabling and about 21% permanent or fatal. 64% is the office figure for permanent or fatal injuries.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement about injuries during monitored anesthesia care is MOST accurate?
options: Nonfatal MAC injuries were usually temporary
MAC carried no fatal claims in the database
MAC injuries were less severe than GA injuries overall
Nonfatal MAC injuries were more often permanent
questions.explanation: Nonfatal injuries during MAC were more likely to be permanent than those during general anesthesia, and about 34% of MAC injuries were fatalities. The other statements contradict those data.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In 1990s ASA closed claims for MAC, what was the MOST common injury type?
questions.explanation: Death was most common (about 34%), followed by brain damage (about 19%), eye damage (about 12%), and nerve damage (about 7%). The distractors pair the right injuries with wrong percentages.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In 1990s ASA closed claims for MAC, about what share of injuries were brain damage?
questions.explanation: Brain damage accounted for about 19%. 34% was death, 12% eye damage, and 7% nerve damage.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which injuries each made up about 4% of MAC closed claims in the 1990s? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: MI, stroke, burns, emotional distress, and aspiration each accounted for about 4%. Eye damage was higher at about 12%.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are the usual causes of morbidity and mortality in office-based anesthesia? (Select 3)
options: Too many staff for the procedure
questions.explanation: Morbidity and mortality in offices usually result from inadequate monitoring, oversedation, or thromboembolism. Oversight is often too little, not too much. Lack of pulse oximetry is the common monitoring failure.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: When office-based injuries involve inadequate monitoring, which monitor is MOST commonly missing?
questions.explanation: Inadequate monitoring, most commonly lack of pulse oximetry, is a leading cause of office injuries. Capnography is also important, but pulse oximetry absence is the most commonly cited failure.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which human-error factors contribute to office-based injuries? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Slow recognition, slow response, inexperience, and overdosage are listed human-error causes. Excess testing and checklists aren't causes of injury.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are recognized causes of injury in office-based practice? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Inadequate resuscitation equipment, inadequate evaluation, inadequate monitoring, and human error are the listed causes. The distractors describe safe practices or non-issues.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: ASA 3 patient with severe COPD wants a mole excision in an office. Which plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Deep sedation with a natural airway
Moderate sedation with careful titration and oxygen
Anesthesia consult, then local without sedation
questions.explanation: ASA 3 patients should undergo office procedures only after an anesthesia consultation and with local anesthesia without sedation. Any sedation adds respiratory risk in this setting.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient is the IDEAL candidate for an office-based procedure?
options: ASA 1 adult with an escort and appropriate fasting
ASA 1 adult with no escort home
ASA 3 adult with COPD wanting deep sedation for comfort
questions.explanation: The ideal office patient is ASA 1 (or 2) with an escort and appropriate fasting. Severe OSA and lack of an escort make a patient unsuitable. ASA 3 patients shouldn't have sedation in an office.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients are UNSUITABLE for an office-based procedure? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes, MH susceptibility, potential difficult airway (morbid obesity, severe OSA), lack of an escort, and substance abuse history are on the unsuitable list. Well-controlled hypertension isn't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients are UNSUITABLE for an office-based procedure? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Seizure disorder, prior adverse anesthetic outcome, significant drug allergies, and solid food within 8 hr are listed contraindications. Stable hypothyroidism is compatible with office care; a minor sensitivity isn't the same as significant drug allergies.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Office procedure is scheduled for 1300. The patient ate a full breakfast with bacon at 0700. Under the office fasting criterion of 8 hr for solids, what is the earliest acceptable start?
questions.explanation: 0700 + 8 hr = 1500. 1300 is 6 hr, acceptable for a light meal by general ASA fasting guidance but not for the office solid-food criterion or a fatty meal. 1100 is 4 hr. 1700 is 10 hr.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient had toast and coffee with cream at 0530 and is scheduled for an office procedure. Using the 8-hr solid-food criterion, when is the earliest start?

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with a large tongue, BMI 46, and STOP-BANG 6 is scheduled for office-based breast augmentation with sedation. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Suitable if propofol is used instead of midazolam
Suitable if the procedure is under 1 hr
questions.explanation: Potential difficult airway, including morbid obesity and severe OSA, makes a patient unsuitable for office-based procedures. Drug choice, oxygen, or a short case doesn't remove the risk in a setting with limited backup.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which procedures are MOST commonly done in office-based settings?
options: Plastic, dental, GYN, urology, and GI cases
Cardiac, thoracic, and major vascular procedures
questions.explanation: Common OBA specialties include urology, gynecology, gastroenterology, ophthalmology, podiatry, dental, and plastic procedures such as liposuction and breast augmentation. The others need hospital resources.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Healthy 3-month-old needs a minor procedure, and the surgeon wants to do it in the office. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Any infant is acceptable if ASA 1
No minimum age exists, but over 6 months is often suggested
Children under 2 years can't have office-based procedures with sedation
Office-based anesthesia is limited to adults
questions.explanation: There is no established minimum age, but over 6 months and ASA 1 or 2 is considered reasonable. A 3-month-old is below that suggestion. Children aren't excluded entirely.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are advantages of office-based anesthesia? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: OBA offers convenience, lower cost, easier scheduling, privacy, and less exposure to hospital infections. Oversight and peer review are often weaker, which is a disadvantage.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are disadvantages of office-based anesthesia? (Select 4)
options: Providers navigate legal, billing, and accreditation issues
Weaker reporting, quality improvement, and peer review
questions.explanation: Safety, reporting, QI, peer review, legal and financial complexity, limited residency training, and variable regulation are disadvantages. OBA is generally cheaper and reduces nosocomial exposure.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: What standard do the ASA and APSF set for office-based anesthesia quality?
options: Lower than a hospital because cases are minor
No less than a hospital or ASC
questions.explanation: ASA and APSF advocate that the quality of care in office-based practice be no less than that of a hospital or ASC.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office wants to offer anesthesia safely. Which elements are required? (Select 5)
options: BLS and ACLS capability with AED, bag-valve mask, and LMA
A plan for transfer to a higher level of care
Permission to skip accreditation if cases are short
DEA-compliant controlled substance storage and waste
questions.explanation: Monitoring, emergency capability, controlled substance security, a medical director, a transfer plan, fire safety, and accreditation by a recognized agency are expected. Accreditation isn't waived for short cases.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which items belong on the required equipment list for office-based anesthesia? (Select 5)
options: Dantrolene and MH supplies when triggers are used
questions.explanation: Required equipment includes monitors, capnography, airway and emergency airway supplies, a video laryngoscope, suction, a defibrillator, ACLS drugs, MH supplies, lipid emulsion if blocks are done, and IV equipment. Bypass isn't expected in an office.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office performs nerve blocks for hand surgery. Which emergency drug must be on hand because of the blocks?
questions.explanation: Intravenous lipid emulsion is required if nerve blocks are performed, to treat local anesthetic toxicity. Dantrolene is required if MH triggers are used. Sugammadex and flumazenil are useful but aren't block-specific requirements.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which emergency airway items are expected in an office-based anesthesia setting? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: LMAs, a cric kit, jet ventilation equipment, and a bag-mask device are listed. Rigid bronchoscopes and double-lumen tubes aren't expected office equipment.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Office uses sevoflurane for a pediatric dental case. Which additional requirement applies?
options: Training and capability to treat MH
An arterial line for every patient having a block
questions.explanation: If MH triggers are used, the office must have training and capability, including dantrolene, to treat MH. The other items aren't required.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Office provides anesthesia using an oxygen cylinder. Which detail is MOST important to confirm?
options: The cylinder is shared with the dental unit
The cylinder key and regulator are present
The cylinder is stored lying flat on the floor
A pipeline backup isn't needed if the cylinder is full
questions.explanation: Offices may rely on cylinders rather than pipeline oxygen, so the key and regulator must be present and working. Cylinders are secured upright. Backup supply planning is still needed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement about capnography for sedation is BEST supported by current ASA guidance?
options: Capnography applies when an anesthesiologist sedates, not others
Capnography is unnecessary if pulse oximetry is used
Capnography is recommended for moderate or deeper sedation
Capnography is required under general anesthesia, not sedation
questions.explanation: ASA monitoring standards require ventilation monitoring with capnography during moderate or deep sedation by anesthesia professionals, and the 2018 ASA practice guidelines for moderate procedural sedation also recommend capnography for non-anesthesiologists. Discrepancy flag: one slide states ASA requires EtCO2 only for sedation by an anesthesiologist; newer guidance extends the recommendation. Pulse oximetry doesn't detect hypoventilation early.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In 2014, which professional group mandated capnography for its members during deep sedation and general anesthesia?
options: American Society of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgeons
American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons
questions.explanation: The AAOMS Board of Trustees mandated capnography for deep sedation and GA in 2014.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which office requirements relate to staffing and supplies? (Select 3)
options: Equipped, staffed, stocked, and maintained to perform GA
Supplies for the planned anesthetic alone
Age- and size-appropriate supplies for the population served
A minimum of one surgeon and no other staff
Adult supplies for every age group
questions.explanation: Offices should be equipped, staffed, and stocked to perform GA, with age-appropriate supplies, and comply with OSHA. Minimal staffing and limited or adult-only supplies don't meet the standard.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Under the ASA office classification, an office that performs minor procedures with local infiltration and no sedation is which class?
questions.explanation: Class A offices perform minor procedures with local, topical, or infiltration anesthesia and no sedation. Class B uses sedation; Class C uses GA or major conduction blocks.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office performs liposuction with oral and IV sedation, including ketamine. What ASA office class applies?
questions.explanation: Class B includes minor or major procedures with oral, rectal, or IV sedation and analgesic or dissociative drugs. Class A uses no sedation. Class C uses GA or major conduction block.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office performs breast augmentation under general anesthesia. What ASA office class applies?
questions.explanation: Class C covers minor or major procedures under GA or major conduction block anesthesia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office performs foot surgery under a popliteal sciatic block with no sedation. Which class fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Class C includes major conduction block anesthesia, which includes plexus and major peripheral nerve blocks. Class A is limited to local, topical, or infiltration without sedation. Class B involves sedation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which features define a Class B office? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Class B offices use sedation by oral, rectal, or IV routes and analgesic or dissociative drugs. GA and major conduction blocks define Class C. No sedation defines Class A.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements describe office-based anesthesia? (Select 2)
options: It occurs in settings not accredited as an ASC or hospital
It's a subset of ambulatory anesthesia
It takes place inside a licensed hospital
It's regulated identically in every state
questions.explanation: OBA is a subset of ambulatory anesthesia in settings not accredited as ASCs or hospitals. Regulation varies by region.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST explains why closed claims data label MAC as more dangerous in office settings?
options: MAC uses more drug than GA in most cases
questions.explanation: Offices often have a provider working alone with limited backup, so oversedation and airway events progress before rescue.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: An office lacks pulse oximetry for a "quick" sedation case. Which cause of office injury does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Lack of pulse oximetry is the most commonly cited monitoring failure in office injuries.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient undergoes office liposuction lasting 4 hr and develops sudden dyspnea and hypoxemia the next day. Which cause of office morbidity is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Thromboembolism is one of the main causes of office morbidity and mortality, especially after long procedures such as liposuction.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements about office anesthesia oversight are accurate? (Select 2)
options: Federal law regulates every office identically
Regulation varies and may be minimal in some regions
Office quality standards are lower by design
Accreditation by a recognized agency is recommended
Peer review is stronger than in hospitals
questions.explanation: ASA and APSF recommend accreditation and quality equal to hospitals; regulation varies regionally.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient is the BEST candidate for an office-based procedure with sedation?
options: ASA 1 adult who ate breakfast 3 hr ago
ASA 2 adult with MH susceptibility using volatile agents
questions.explanation: Healthy ASA 1–2 patients who are fasted and have an escort are ideal. ASA 3 patients shouldn't receive sedation in offices, recent solids disqualify, and MH susceptibility is unsuitable.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: During colonoscopy, a patient responds purposefully to verbal commands with light tactile stimulation, maintains a patent airway, and breathes adequately. What level of sedation is this?
questions.explanation: Purposeful response to verbal commands, alone or with light touch, with an intact airway and spontaneous ventilation, defines moderate sedation. Minimal sedation responds normally to verbal commands. Deep sedation requires repeated or painful stimulation. GA isn't arousable to pain.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient responds normally to voice, is a little slow to answer questions, and breathes normally after oral diazepam. What level of sedation is this?
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation (anxiolysis) means normal response to verbal commands; cognition and coordination may be impaired, while ventilation and circulation are unaffected.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient during propofol sedation can't be easily roused but withdraws and moans purposefully to repeated painful stimulation. A jaw thrust is needed to keep the airway open. What level of sedation is this?
questions.explanation: Deep sedation means the patient can't be easily roused but responds purposefully to repeated or painful stimulation, and airway support may be needed. Reflex withdrawal alone isn't purposeful; if the patient weren't arousable to pain, it would be GA.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient during propofol infusion doesn't respond to a firm trapezius squeeze, and the ventilator is needed for adequate breathing. What level of anesthesia is this?
questions.explanation: Loss of consciousness without arousal to painful stimulation, with impaired ventilation often needing positive pressure, defines GA. Deep sedation still allows purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements describe deep sedation? (Select 3)
options: Positive pressure ventilation is often required
Not arousable even to painful stimulation
May need help maintaining a patent airway
Not easily roused but responds purposefully to repeated or painful stimulation
questions.explanation: Deep sedation features arousal only with repeated or painful stimulation, possible airway support, possibly inadequate spontaneous ventilation, and usually maintained circulation. Normal response to voice is minimal sedation. Unarousable patients needing PPV are under GA.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements describe general anesthesia? (Select 4)
options: Patient responds purposefully to light touch
Positive pressure ventilation is often required
questions.explanation: GA means drug-induced loss of consciousness without arousal to pain, often impaired ventilation and neuromuscular function, frequent need for PPV, and possible cardiovascular impairment. Responding to light touch is moderate sedation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient getting moderate sedation for endoscopy now requires a chin lift to stop obstruction and responds only to a firm sternal rub. Which statement BEST describes what happened?
options: Sedation has deepened beyond the intended level
This is general anesthesia because airway support is needed
This is minimal sedation with a positional airway
questions.explanation: Needing airway support and responding only to painful stimulation signals deep sedation. Sedation is a continuum, so providers must be able to rescue patients from deeper levels than intended. GA would mean no purposeful response to pain.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: At which level of sedation is cardiovascular function described as "maintained," with a patent airway and adequate spontaneous ventilation?
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation maintains airway patency, spontaneous ventilation, and cardiovascular function. In deep sedation cardiovascular function is "usually" maintained, and in GA it may be impaired.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which findings fit minimal sedation (anxiolysis)? (Select 3)
options: Needs light tactile stimulation to respond
Possible impairment of cognition and coordination
questions.explanation: Anxiolysis preserves normal responses to voice and normal ventilation and circulation, though cognition and coordination may be impaired. Needing touch to respond is moderate sedation. Airway support and pain-only response describe deeper levels.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which finding is NOT considered a purposeful response when judging sedation depth?
options: Following a command to squeeze a hand
Pushing the provider's hand away from the face
Reflex withdrawal from a painful stimulus
questions.explanation: Reflex withdrawal from pain isn't a purposeful response; purposeful responses include following commands or reaching to push away a stimulus. Distinguishing these separates deep sedation from GA.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Endoscopist without anesthesia training wants to give propofol for "light sedation" in an office. What is the main concern?
options: Propofol has no respiratory effects at low doses
Propofol can't produce sedation lighter than GA
Propofol is reversed easily with flumazenil
Propofol can quickly produce deep sedation or GA
questions.explanation: Propofol has a narrow margin and can move a patient from intended sedation to deep sedation or GA rapidly, requiring rescue skills. Low doses can sedate lightly, but respiratory depression occurs, and there is no reversal agent.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: For which sedation levels is airway intervention possibly needed? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Deep sedation may require airway support, and GA often does. Minimal and moderate sedation maintain a patent airway by definition.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: In which setting does closed claims data suggest MAC is especially dangerous?
options: Office-based practice working remotely with limited backup
ICU settings with continuous monitoring by dedicated nurses
questions.explanation: MAC injuries were frequently permanent or fatal, and office settings add isolation and limited backup, making oversedation more dangerous there. Hospital settings provide more support.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why might nonfatal injuries during MAC be more likely to be permanent than those during GA?
options: MAC uses higher drug doses than GA
GA patients are healthier than MAC patients
MAC is given by non-anesthesia providers
questions.explanation: Oversedation with respiratory depression and an unprotected airway can lead to hypoxic brain injury, which is often permanent. MAC doesn't use higher doses, patient health doesn't explain it, and anesthesia professionals frequently provide MAC.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which elements of governance should an office anesthesia practice have? (Select 3)
options: A requirement that surgeons give their own sedation
Accreditation by a nationally recognized agency
questions.explanation: A medical director, accreditation, and escalation and transfer plans are expected. Surgeons giving their own sedation, skipping fire safety, and limited reporting weaken safety.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient in an office develops refractory hypotension after a block. Which preparation would have mattered MOST?
options: A second surgeon in the room
A plan for transfer to a higher level of care
A prescription for oral analgesics before discharge
questions.explanation: Offices need a defined process for escalation and transfer to a hospital. The other items don't address deteriorating patients.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why is office-based anesthesia NOT typically part of residency training?
options: Office cases are too complex for trainees
Office anesthesia doesn't require special knowledge
Office anesthesia is illegal for trainees
Most programs train in hospitals and ASCs
questions.explanation: Training programs center on hospitals and ASCs, so OBA practice issues (regulation, staffing, billing, accreditation) are often learned after training. It isn't illegal or excessively complex, and it does require specific knowledge.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: A colleague says an office procedure is "just a Class A case." Which plan is consistent with that class?
questions.explanation: Class A offices use only local, topical, or infiltration anesthesia without pre- or intraoperative sedation. Any sedation, including oral premedication, moves it to Class B.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement about office classes is MOST accurate?
options: Class A offices may provide general anesthesia if brief
Class reflects the deepest anesthesia allowed
Class C is limited to topical anesthesia
Class B offices may perform major conduction blocks
questions.explanation: ASA classes stratify offices by the depth of anesthesia they may provide. Class A has no sedation; Class B allows sedation; Class C allows GA and major conduction blocks. Discrepancy flag: a note in the course materials pairs Class A with office settings and Classes B and C with surgery centers or hospitals; the classification itself applies to offices, which may qualify for any class if properly equipped and accredited.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: During an office case under moderate sedation, SpO2 drops from 98% to 89%. Capnography shows a flat line, and there is no chest rise. What is the FIRST action?
options: Increase nasal cannula oxygen to 6 L/min and observe
Give naloxone and wait for response
Stop the infusion, open the airway, ventilate
questions.explanation: A flat capnogram with no chest movement means apnea or complete obstruction; airway maneuvers and positive pressure ventilation come first. Increasing oxygen or rechecking equipment delays rescue. Reversal agents can follow once ventilation is restored.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which monitoring change would MOST likely have detected hypoventilation earliest during office sedation with supplemental oxygen?
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen delays desaturation, so capnography reveals hypoventilation before SpO2 falls. Blood pressure and temperature don't detect ventilatory changes.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which preparations are reasonable before office-based sedation in a healthy patient? (Select 4)
options: Skip the airway exam because sedation is planned
Omit an IV because sedation will be oral
questions.explanation: Fasting, escort, prior anesthetic history, and equipment checks are basic safety steps. An airway exam is still needed because sedation can deepen. IV access is standard even with oral sedation in many settings.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST explains why office-based injuries tend to be more severe?
options: Limited backup, monitoring, and resources slow rescue
Office procedures are longer than hospital procedures
Office patients are sicker than hospital patients
Office anesthetics use more potent drugs
questions.explanation: Offices often lack the backup personnel, equipment, and oversight that allow rapid rescue, so events progress further. Office patients are typically healthier.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are recognized NORA and office-based safety priorities? (Select 3)
options: Using deep sedation to shorten procedures
Rescue capability for deeper levels than intended
Relying on the surgeon to monitor sedation
questions.explanation: Patient selection, standard monitoring, and the ability to rescue from deeper sedation are central priorities. The distractors undermine safety.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: At which levels is cardiovascular function described as maintained or usually maintained? (Select 3)
options: Any level when an opioid is given
Unresponsive patient after propofol bolus with hypotension
questions.explanation: Minimal and moderate sedation maintain cardiovascular function, and deep sedation usually does. GA may impair it.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient during sedation needs positive pressure ventilation and doesn't respond to pain. What depth and implication?
options: Moderate sedation; continue the same plan
questions.explanation: Unarousable patients needing PPV are under GA, which requires airway management.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient sedated for bronchoscopy follows commands slowly but correctly when spoken to, with normal breathing. What level?
questions.explanation: Normal response to verbal commands, even if slowed, indicates minimal sedation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which response best separates moderate from deep sedation?
options: Eye opening versus no eye opening to spoken commands
Voice or light touch versus repeated or painful stimuli
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation responds to voice or light touch; deep sedation requires repeated or painful stimulation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which features separate deep sedation from general anesthesia? (Select 2)
options: Purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation
questions.explanation: Deep sedation still allows purposeful response to painful stimulation; GA doesn't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient needs anesthesia for ECT in the psychiatry suite of a licensed hospital. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: ECT within a licensed hospital outside the OR is a NORA location.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements about NORA are accurate? (Select 2)
options: It occurs outside a traditional OR
It occurs inside a fully licensed hospital
It occurs in freestanding surgery centers
questions.explanation: NORA occurs outside the OR within a licensed hospital, including imaging and endoscopy suites.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which recovery consideration applies to NORA patients?
options: They're discharged from the procedure table
questions.explanation: NORA patients recover in a setting appropriate to their acuity.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank
